title: A spiral in Andromeda
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7640, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 7640 · constellation Andromeda · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble image shows NGC 7640, a galaxy in the constellation of Andromeda. The name can cause confusion, since the constellation is one of the 88 modern constellations and not to be mixed up with our neighbour the Andromeda Galaxy.

Astronomers sort galaxies by shape and structure, and NGC 7640 is a barred spiral. In galaxies of this type, the spiral arms fan out not from a round core but from an elongated bar that runs through the centre. Our own Milky Way is a barred spiral too.

NGC 7640 may not look much like a spiral here. That is because of the angle from which we, and Hubble, see it. Galaxies are rarely turned face-on towards us, and when they are tilted, features such as spiral arms become harder to make out.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.32 x 3.34 arcminutes) and distance (30 million light years), the frame spans roughly 29,000 × 29,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble shows fine structure that no eye at a telescope could pick out.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: NGC 7640 lies about 30 million light-years away. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys in visible and near-infrared light.
alt: A tilted spiral galaxy seen at an angle, so its arms are hard to make out.
